solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Bowl over toilet? Not quite fun (6)

indicatorNotes.Not quite: Not quite all of it means the word stops one letter short, so GLEE loses its last E.

blocks.note: bog is British slang for a toilet
glee = fun, merriment; cut short to GLE

annotation.surface: A grumble that cleaning round the toilet bowl is not much fun.
annotation.walkthrough: "Bowl over toilet" paints a lavatory bowl, but "Bowl over" is the definition, meaning to astonish.
annotation.definitionFit: To boggle someone is to overwhelm them with amazement, as to bowl them over is.

indicatorNotes.in: Z is put in among the rearranged letters.
indicatorNotes.ordered: To order things is to arrange them, so the letters of TRIBUNAL are rearranged.

blocks.note: the first letter of Zulu, which is the NATO alphabet word for that letter
rearranged around the Z

annotation.surface: A court orders a Zulu to hand over some fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: A Brazil nut is botanically a seed, but crosswords and greengrocers count it as fruit.
annotation.definitionFit: The Brazil nut is the large edible seed of a South American tree, sold with fruit and nuts.

blocks.note: to get something is to see it, as in "I got the joke"
op. = opus, a work
OT = Old Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: A carpenter's saw, a worker's books: everything is falling apart.
annotation.walkthrough: "Saw" reads as the tool, but it is the past tense of see, in the sense of understood. The pieces ignore the answer's own word breaks.
annotation.definitionFit: To go to pot is to decline badly, to go to ruin.

indicatorNotes.in: The answer sits inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: newcastLE PERhaps

annotation.surface: Someone unwelcome in Newcastle, perhaps.
annotation.walkthrough: "Newcastle, perhaps" looks like a city given as an example; it only holds the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A leper, figuratively, is an outcast whom everyone avoids: an undesirable.
annotation.definitionNote: "Undesirable" is used as a noun here: an undesirable person.

indicatorNotes.in: PC and O go in STOCK, splitting it STO...CK.

blocks.note: stock = the goods a shop holds, its inventory
a copper is a policeman, a PC (police constable)
O is ring-shaped

annotation.surface: A plumber's list of spare parts includes a copper ring for a valve.
annotation.walkthrough: Copper and a ring look like plumbing parts in a valve; here copper is a policeman. The 's stands for "is".
annotation.definitionFit: A stopcock is a valve that turns the water supply in a pipe on or off.

indicatorNotes.broadcast: To broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters are scattered and rearranged.

blocks.note: the letters rearranged

annotation.surface: Preachers promise to televise the events they stage.
annotation.walkthrough: "Broadcast" fits the answer too: televangelists preach on TV.
annotation.definitionFit: Televangelists are preachers who spread their message through television.

entries.clue: Temple woman: That is one way to feed crowd (9)

indicatorNotes.to feed: Food goes inside whatever is fed, so IE and ST go into PRESS.

blocks.note: a press is a crowd pushing together
i.e. = id est, that is
a street, St, is one kind of way

annotation.surface: A woman at the temple explains the right way to feed the crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon suggests the woman is speaking; she is the definition, and her "words" are the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A priestess is a woman who performs the rites in a temple.

entries.clue: Fruit variety with very large skin (7)

indicatorNotes.skin: A skin wraps round what it covers, so OS goes round RANGE.

blocks.note: OS = outsize, a clothing label for very large
a range is a variety, as in a range of goods

annotation.surface: A kind of fruit notable for its very large skin.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a pomelo; "skin" is a verb here, telling one piece to wrap round the other.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the orange is one of the commonest citrus fruits, and "Fruit" is read as a plural.

entries.clue: Ring from King Charles II’s lover (5)

blocks.note: K = king, as in chess
Nell Gwyn was King Charles II's famous mistress

annotation.surface: A ring given to Charles II by his mistress.
annotation.walkthrough: "Ring" suggests jewellery a lover might give; it means the sound of a bell.
annotation.definitionFit: A knell is the ring of a bell, especially one tolled for a death.

indicatorNotes.excitedly: Things done excitedly are thrown about, so the letters are jumbled.

blocks.note: letters to rearrange
more letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: People from Moravia breed with each other and chase game in a frenzy.
annotation.walkthrough: Moravia is a region of the Czech Republic, but the Moravian Church, also called the United Brethren, is a Protestant denomination.
annotation.definitionFit: The Moravian Church is formally the Unitas Fratrum, the United Brethren, so its members are Moravians.

entries.clue: In a run, with two to go? (15)

annotation.definition: In a run, with two to go?

blocks.note: the surface suggests running or a cricket run; the setter means placed in a sequence
two more items still come after this one, so it is third from last

annotation.surface: A runner in a race, or a batter at the crease, with two more to go.
annotation.walkthrough: The run is a sequence, not a jog or a cricket run: an item with two more after it is the antepenultimate one.
annotation.definitionFit: Antepenultimate means third from last, so two items remain after it.

indicatorNotes.bats: Bats means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange.

blocks.note: letters to rearrange
more letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A spooky place gives orders, crawling with vampire bats.
annotation.walkthrough: "Vampire bats" looks like one animal; "bats" is a separate word meaning crazy.
annotation.definitionFit: Imperatives are commands, and the imperative is the grammatical mood of command.

indicatorNotes.heading west: In an across clue, going west is reading right to left, so LAG turns into GAL.

blocks.note: an old lag is a long-serving convict

annotation.surface: A woman convict making her escape westward.
annotation.walkthrough: An old lag is British slang for a habitual prisoner.
annotation.definitionFit: Gal is an informal word for a girl or woman.
annotation.definitionNote: "Female" is used as a noun: a female person.

blocks.note: a step or grade on a scale, as when someone moves up a level
to score is to cut a small mark into a surface

annotation.surface: A demand to even up the score.
annotation.walkthrough: "Level score" reads as a draw; it is two words, each meaning NOTCH.
annotation.definitionFit: A notch is both a step up (a level) and a cut (a score) in a surface.

blocks.note: easily, without any contest, like a race won by a mile
to hand down is to pass on, as in a will

annotation.surface: Someone just walks out.
annotation.walkthrough: "Leaves" looks like departs or foliage; it means bequeaths, as a parent hands down an heirloom.
annotation.definitionFit: Hands down means easily, simply; hands down means bequeaths, leaves to an heir.

entries.clue: Table service from daughter and close friends? (6,3)

blocks.note: d = daughter, as in family trees
an inner set is one's circle of close friends

annotation.surface: A family's plates and dishes, a gift from their daughter and close friends.
annotation.walkthrough: "Service" is a set of matching crockery here, not help from waiters.
annotation.definitionFit: A dinner set is a matching set of plates and dishes for the table, also called a dinner service.

entries.clue: Spiked thing in grooves on tiller (5,4)

blocks.note: tracks are the grooves on a record
a hoe tills the soil

annotation.surface: A spiked tool sits in grooves on a farmer's tiller.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue, "on" puts TRACKS above HOE. A tiller also steers a boat; here it is whatever tills soil.
annotation.definitionFit: A track shoe is a running shoe with spikes in the sole for grip.

entries.clue: May perhaps enter violently, chasing one with hammer (9)

indicatorNotes.violently: Letters treated violently are knocked out of order, so ENTER is rearranged.
indicatorNotes.chasing: What chases comes behind, so the rearranged ENTER follows THOR.

blocks.note: Thor, the Norse god of thunder, wields a hammer
rearranged as NTREE

annotation.surface: Someone may break in violently, pursuing a man armed with a hammer.
annotation.walkthrough: "May" is the hawthorn, named for when it flowers, not the modal verb or the month; "perhaps" flags it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: May, or hawthorn, is a thorny tree, so it is one kind of thorn tree.

entries.clue: Sea being cold, to work outside (7)

indicatorNotes.outside: OPUS goes outside C and TO, holding them.

blocks.note: an opus is a work, especially of music
C = cold, as on a tap
used as it is

annotation.surface: The sea is cold, so it's time to work outdoors.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sea being cold" reads as a statement about the water; "Sea being" is the definition, a creature of the sea.
annotation.definitionFit: An octopus is an eight-armed creature that lives in the sea.

indicatorNotes.returned: To return is to go back, so AMGIS is read backwards.

blocks.note: Am. = American
GIs are American soldiers

annotation.surface: A letter sent back by American troops.
annotation.walkthrough: "American soldiers" looks like one idea, GIs; it is AM + GIS, the whole reversed.
annotation.definitionFit: Sigma is the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: Stew pan out with superior batter (7)

blocks.note: to pan out is to turn out, as things go
U = upper-class, superior
to batter is to beat, to lash

annotation.surface: A cook makes stew, then pours superior batter from the pan.
annotation.walkthrough: "Pan" and "batter" suggest cooking; "pan out" means turn out, GO, and batter means beat.
annotation.definitionFit: Goulash is a Hungarian stew of meat and paprika.

blocks.note: O = old
FT = Financial Times, a newspaper

annotation.surface: A big pile of old newspapers.
annotation.walkthrough: "A lot of" reads as a quantity of paper; "A lot" means frequently, and "of" joins.
annotation.definitionFit: Oft is an old word for often, a lot.
annotation.definitionNote: "A lot" is used adverbially, as in "we go there a lot", matching OFT.

indicatorNotes.leader leaves: The leader is the first letter; when it leaves, BOTHER loses its B.

blocks.note: to upset is to bother; that word then loses its first letter

annotation.surface: People get more upset once the leader resigns.
annotation.walkthrough: "More upset" reads as one phrase; "More" is the definition, as in "other" meaning additional.
annotation.definitionFit: Other can mean additional, more, as in "a few other things".

entries.clue: Spell “circumvent” — this should be a pushover (7,4)

blocks.note: a sitting is a spell or session, as for a portrait
to duck an issue is to avoid it, circumvent it

annotation.surface: A spelling test on the word "circumvent" should be easy.
annotation.walkthrough: "Spell" looks like an instruction to spell a word, and the quote marks look like the word to spell; they are two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A sitting duck is an easy target, someone who should be a pushover.
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a phrase describing the answer: a sitting duck is something that should be a pushover.

entries.clue: Fine clubs, say, over climbing reptile (5)

indicatorNotes.over: Over means turned over, so the three pieces are read upward, in reverse.

blocks.note: OK = fine
C = clubs, the card suit
e.g. = for example, say

annotation.surface: Fine clubs, for example, laid over a reptile as it climbs.
annotation.walkthrough: "Climbing" looks like the reversal indicator in a down clue, but it belongs to the definition: geckos climb walls. "Over" does the reversing.
annotation.definitionFit: A gecko is a small lizard whose sticky toe pads let it climb walls and ceilings.

blocks.note: doctors
the surface means trust it completely; the setter means take a solemn oath on it

annotation.surface: Doctors vouch for a remedy they trust.
annotation.walkthrough: To swear by something usually means to trust it completely; here doctors literally swear by the oath.
annotation.definitionFit: The Hippocratic oath is the ethical oath taken by doctors, named after the Greek physician Hippocrates.

indicatorNotes.about: About means turned round, so NOSE is read backwards as ESON.
indicatorNotes.gathering: To gather something is to take it in, so RANT holds ESON.

blocks.note: to storm is to rant and rage
a nose is a knack for perceiving, as in a nose for news

annotation.surface: A deep sense that a storm is gathering.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's stands for "has": RANT has ESON inside it. RANT splits R...ANT.
annotation.definitionFit: A resonant voice or sound is deep and full, echoing on.

entries.clue: Kind of finch to circle endlessly (6)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Without its end, WHEEL loses its last letter to become WHEE.

blocks.note: used as it is
to wheel is to circle, as birds do; the word then loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A finch that flies round in circles without stopping.
annotation.walkthrough: "Circle endlessly" suggests a bird wheeling for ever; "endlessly" means cut off the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The towhee is a North American bird of the finch-like sparrow family, named for its call.
